title: Advantages and Limitations of Docker
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of advantages and limitations of docker.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to advantages and limitations of docker.
Predict an expected result and verify it using observable evidence in a controlled environment.

content.intro: This lesson covers Advantages and Limitations of Docker. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Treat advantages and limitations of docker as a behavior to explain and verify, not a command to memorize. Identify the Docker component or setting involved, predict the outcome, then confirm it using a small isolated lab and a recorded result. Learning advantages and limitations of docker helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

items.title: Portability and reproducibility
items.text: A container port and a published host port are different values. Bind publishing deliberately, especially when a service should be reachable only from the local machine.

items.title: Resource efficiency
items.text: Measure the workload under a repeatable baseline and change one variable at a time. Resource options and observed enforcement can differ by platform.

items.title: Dependency management
items.text: For dependency management, name the relevant Docker object, setting, or operational step; predict its effect; and capture evidence from a controlled test or inspection command. Relate the result back to advantages and limitations of docker rather than assuming that a successful command proves the wider system is correct.

items.text: Reduce privileges to the minimum required, then run the intended application workflow to catch permission assumptions; container hardening is platform- and workload-dependent.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with the supplied example for advantages and limitations of docker. Before running it, state what you expect to happen. Compare the real output with that prediction, then change one variable or setting in a disposable lab to test the boundary of the idea. If a command is not supported on your operating system or installed Docker version, consult the linked official reference and record the actual version rather than guessing.

task: Apply advantages and limitations of docker to a small local case. Record the configuration or command, expected result, observed result, one limitation/edge case, and how you verified the result.
hints: Begin with read-only inspection commands and identify the active Docker context before any mutating action.
Use a disposable name, local test image, and synthetic data; change one thing at a time.
If the outcome differs, preserve the exact error and logs, check the official reference for your installed version, and document the verified fix.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
